Chapter 6: Releasing the Habit of Minimizing and Embracing a Stronger Presence.
As our journey continues, let’s shine a light on a habit that can really hold us back—even if we don’t always notice it. It’s called minimizing. Have you ever caught yourself shrinking your ideas, softening your words, or literally making yourself smaller in a group? You’re not alone.
Minimizing can slip into our lives in all sorts of ways. Maybe you’ve said things like, “I just wanted to add…” or, “This might be a silly question, but…” Sometimes, it shows up in our bodies—hunched shoulders, eyes darting away, or quietly sitting on the edge in meetings.
Why do we do this? Most of the time, it’s something we’ve learned—maybe from being in places where assertiveness wasn’t welcome, or where standing out felt risky. But here’s the thing: all those little moments where we hold back send a message—not just to others, but to ourselves—that what we have to say doesn’t matter as much.
So, how do you break the habit of minimizing? It starts with learning to truly occupy your space. Now, I’m not talking about taking over conversations or ignoring others. It’s about showing up fully—letting yourself be seen and heard, just as you are.
Picture this: you walk into a room and take a seat at the table, instead of hovering at the edge. Or, when you share an idea, you say it clearly and confidently—no shrinking, no apologies.
Here are a few gentle shifts you can try:
First, swap out minimizing words for clear, direct ones. Instead of, “I just think…” try, “I recommend…” It’s a small change, but it really lands differently.
Next, practice open, grounded body language. Shoulders back, steady eye contact, and a relaxed posture can make a world of difference in how you feel—and how others see you.
Before your next meeting, think of one or two points you want to contribute. Then, commit to sharing them. It’s a simple way to build your presence, one step at a time.
And if you catch yourself shrinking or wanting to apologize for your ideas? Pause for a moment. Take a breath. Give yourself permission to reset and show up fully.
Little by little, these small changes add up. Over time, you’ll notice you feel stronger in your presence, and others will notice, too. You’re letting the world see the real you—and that’s what shifts the energy in meetings, in collaborations, and in life.
Remember, overcoming minimizing isn’t about pretending to be someone else. It’s about giving your authentic self a chance to be seen and heard. And that’s a gift worth sharing.
